IGCSE Physics - Chapter 9: Magnets & Currents (1-8)

Question 1 (0625/41_Summer_2017_Q8) - Magnets And Currents

A bar magnet is made of metal.

(a) Suggest a metal from which the bar magnet is made. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

The bar magnet is made from a hard magnetic material such as steel.

(b) Fig. 8.1 shows the bar magnet being inserted into a coil of wire. The N-pole and the S-pole of the bar magnet are marked.

The coil is connected to a galvanometer.

(i) Explain why the galvanometer deflects as the bar magnet is being inserted into the coil. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

As the magnet moves, its magnetic field lines are cut by the coil. This change in magnetic flux linkage induces an electromotive force (e.m.f.) across the coil, causing a current to flow and the galvanometer to deflect.

(ii) Explain what determines the direction of the reading on the galvanometer. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

The direction of the induced e.m.f. is determined by the direction of movement of the magnet and which pole of the magnet enters the coil. The induced e.m.f. will create a magnetic field that opposes the change causing it.

(c) Describe a method for demagnetising a bar magnet. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

One method is to place the magnet inside a coil carrying an alternating current (a.c.). Then, with the current still on, the magnet is slowly removed from the coil to a great distance, or the current is slowly decreased to zero.

Question 2 (0625/42_Summer_2017_Q9) - Magnets And Currents

Fig. 9.1 shows a horizontal wire PQ placed in the gap between the N pole and the S pole of a magnet.

There is a current in the wire in the direction P to Q. A force acts on the current-carrying wire in the magnetic field.

(a) On Fig. 9.1, draw

(i) an arrow, labelled M to show the direction of the magnetic field in the gap between the poles of the magnet, [1]

(ii) an arrow, labelled F to show the direction of the force on the current-carrying wire due to the magnetic field of the magnet. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

(i) The arrow M should be drawn from the N pole to the S pole, pointing horizontally from left to right.

(ii) Using Fleming's Left-Hand Rule, the arrow F should be drawn pointing downwards.

(b) State the effect of reversing the direction of the current in wire PQ. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

The direction of the force on the wire will be reversed; it will now act upwards.

(c) The magnet is removed and the horizontal, current-carrying wire is left on its own, as shown in Fig. 9.2.

(i) On Fig. 9.2, sketch the pattern of the magnetic field due to the current in the wire. Indicate the field direction. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

The sketch should show at least three concentric circles centered on the wire. Using the right-hand grip rule, the direction of the field lines should be clockwise.

(ii) The current in PQ is increased. State the effect of this change in current on the magnetic field. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

The magnetic field becomes stronger, and the field lines become closer together.

(d) A small magnet is placed at a point where the magnetic field is vertically upwards. State the direction of the force on the S pole of the small magnet. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

The force on an S pole is opposite to the direction of the magnetic field, so the force will be directed vertically downwards.

Question 3 (0625/43_Summer_2017_Q10) - Magnets And Currents

Fig. 10.1 shows a transformer that consists of two coils P and Q, and an iron core.

There are 200 turns on coil P and 340 turns on coil Q. A 4.0V a.c. power supply is connected to coil P.

(a) (i) Explain why there is a voltage between the two terminals of coil Q. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

The alternating current in coil P produces a changing magnetic field in the iron core. This changing field is linked to coil Q, and through electromagnetic induction, a voltage is induced in coil Q.

(ii) Explain why the core of the transformer is made of soft iron. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

Soft iron is used because it is an easily magnetised and demagnetised material, making it a temporary magnet that can efficiently transfer the changing magnetic field.

(b) (i) Calculate the voltage between the two terminals of coil Q. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Vs ⁄ Vp = Ns ⁄ Np

Vs = Vp × (Ns ⁄ Np) = 4.0V × (340 ⁄ 200) = 6.8V

The voltage is 6.8 V.

(ii) A heater is connected to coil Q. The current in the heater is 3.5A. The transformer is 100% efficient. Calculate the current in coil P. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

IpVp = IsVs

Ip = (IsVs) ⁄ Vp = (3.5A × 6.8V) ⁄ 4.0V = 5.95A

The current is 6.0 A.

(c) A transformer is used to step up the voltage before electrical energy is transmitted over long distances. State and explain one economic effect of transmitting electrical energy at a high voltage. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Transmitting at a high voltage allows for a lower current, which means less energy is wasted as heat in the cables. This makes the system more efficient and cheaper to run, as less fuel is required at the power station, and thinner, less expensive cables can be used.

Question 4 (0625/43_Winter_2017_Q9) - Magnets And Currents

(a) Fig. 9.1 shows the structure of an alternating current (a.c.) generator.

The coil completes one rotation every 0.020s.

(i) Using the axes in Fig. 9.2, sketch a graph to show how the voltage output of the generator varies with time during a period of 0.040s. [2]

(ii) On your graph in Fig. 9.2, mark a point labelled A to indicate a time when the coil is vertical. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

(i) The graph should be a sine or cosine curve with a period of 0.020s, showing two complete cycles within the 0.040s timeframe. The maximum and minimum voltage values should be equal in magnitude.

(ii) Point A should be marked where the output voltage is zero, as this occurs when the coil is vertical and moving parallel to the magnetic field.

(b) There is an alternating current (a.c.) in a horizontal wire that is buried in a wall. A builder must miss this wire when drilling a hole in the wall. The builder places an instrument against the wall that registers a reading when it is close to the wire. The instrument includes a long coil (solenoid) S that has an iron core and a sensitive voltmeter. Fig. 9.3 shows the circuit of the instrument close to the wire.

(i) Explain why there is a reading on the voltmeter. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

The alternating current in the buried wire creates a changing magnetic field around it. This changing field cuts through the solenoid S, inducing an e.m.f. (voltage) in the coil, which is detected by the voltmeter.

(ii) State the name and the effect of the component labelled X in Fig. 9.3. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Component X is a diode. Its effect is to rectify the alternating current, meaning it allows current to flow in only one direction.

Question 5 (0625/41_Winter_2017_Q10) - Magnets And Currents, Electron And Electronics

(a) (i) Draw the circuit symbol for a diode. [1]

(ii) State the function of a diode. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

(i) The symbol should be a triangle pointing towards a vertical line.

(ii) The function is to allow current to flow in only one direction.

(b) Fig. 10.1 shows the proposed system for charging the battery of an electric toothbrush.

The handle of the brush contains the battery and a coil X. The circuit from coil X to the battery is not shown. The base of the charger contains a coil Y, wound on an iron core, connected to the a.c. mains supply. To charge the battery, the handle is lowered so that coil Y is inside coil X. Fig. 10.1 shows the direction needed for the charging current at the battery.

(i) On Fig. 10.1, complete the circuit from terminals A and B of coil X to the battery. Include a diode. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

A wire should connect from terminal B to the positive (+) terminal of the battery. A wire should connect from terminal A to the negative (-) terminal. A diode must be included in this circuit, oriented to allow current to flow in at the positive terminal.

(ii) Explain how an alternating voltage is produced in coil X. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

The alternating current in coil Y sets up an alternating magnetic field. This changing magnetic flux cuts through or links with coil X. By electromagnetic induction, an alternating voltage is induced in coil X.

Question 6 (0625/42_Winter_2017_Q10) - Magnets And Currents

(a) Fig. 10.1 shows a wire that carries a current into the page. The circles on Fig. 10.1 show the pattern of the magnetic field around the wire.

(i) On Fig. 10.1, draw an arrow on each circle to show the direction of the magnetic field. [1]

(ii) State why the spacing of the circles increases as the distance from the wire increases. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

(i) Using the right-hand grip rule, the arrows on the circles should point in a clockwise direction.

(ii) The spacing increases because the magnetic field becomes weaker with increasing distance from the wire.

(b) Fig. 10.2 shows an electric door lock. The slot in the door contains an unmagnetised iron bolt attached to a spring. The slot in the door frame is empty. This slot is surrounded by the coils of a solenoid. In Fig. 10.2 the door is unlocked. The spring is not stretched.

In Fig. 10.3 the door is locked. The spring is now stretched.

The bolt is initially in the position shown in Fig. 10.2. Describe and explain what happens when

(i) the switch S is closed, [4]

Tap to reveal answer

When the switch is closed, a current flows in the solenoid, turning it into an electromagnet. This magnetises the iron bolt. The solenoid attracts the bolt, causing it to move into the solenoid, stretching the spring and locking the door.

(ii) the switch S is reopened. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

When the switch is opened, the current stops, and the solenoid and bolt are no longer magnetised. The stretched spring contracts and pulls the bolt back to its original position, unlocking the door.

Question 7 (0625/41_Summer_2018_Q9) - Magnets And Currents

(a) A student wants to demagnetise a permanent bar magnet. She suggests these steps:

  1. Place the magnet in a long coil.
  2. Switch on a large alternating current in the coil.
  3. Switch off the current.
  4. Remove the bar from the coil.

State and explain whether the steps will always be able to demagnetise the magnet. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

No, this method will not be effective. The magnet should be withdrawn from the coil while the alternating current is still on. Switching the current off while the magnet is inside will leave it magnetised in the direction of the field at the instant the current was switched off.

(b) (i) Fig. 9.1 shows a coil supplied with current using a split-ring commutator.

State and explain any motion of the coil. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

The coil will turn continuously in a clockwise direction. This is due to the force on the current in the magnetic field. The split-ring commutator reverses the direction of the current in the coil every half turn, ensuring the turning force remains in the same direction.

(ii) The coil in Fig. 9.1 consists of three turns of wire. The magnetic field strength of the magnet is M. With a current of 2.0A in the coil, the coil experiences a turning effect T. The first row of Table 9.1 shows this data. Complete Table 9.1 to give the turning effect for the changes made to the arrangement shown in Fig. 9.1. Choose your answers from the box. [3]

T⁄8     T⁄4     T⁄2     T     2T     4T     8T
number of turns current in the coil/A magnetic field strength turning effect
3 2.0 M T
3 8.0 M
6 2.0 M
3 2.0 M⁄2
Tap to reveal answer

Row 2: Current is 4 times larger (8.0⁄2.0), so turning effect is 4T.

Row 3: Number of turns is 2 times larger (6⁄3), so turning effect is 2T.

Row 4: Field strength is halved, so turning effect is T⁄2.

Question 8 (0625/42_Summer_2018_Q9) - Magnets And Currents

(a) Fig. 9.1 shows a coil ABCD with two turns. The coil is in a magnetic field.

When there is a current in the coil, the coil experiences a turning effect.

(i) Explain why there is a turning effect. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

There are forces on sides AB and CD which are in opposite vertical directions, creating a turning couple.

(ii) The value of the current is 3A. Place one tick in each column of the table to indicate how the turning effect changes with the change described. [3]

change decreased by factor of 4 decreased by factor of 3 decreased by factor of 2 no change increased by factor of 2 increased by factor of 3 increased by factor of 4
number of turns on coil increased to six
current increased to 9A
strength of magnetic field decreased by a factor of 2
Tap to reveal answer

Row 1: Turns increased from 2 to 6 (factor of 3). Tick increased by factor of 3.

Row 2: Current increased from 3A to 9A (factor of 3). Tick increased by factor of 3.

Row 3: Field strength decreased by factor of 2. Tick decreased by factor of 2.

(b) Fig. 9.2 shows a magnet held just below a vertical coil connected to a galvanometer.

The magnet is released.

(i) State any effect on the galvanometer. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

The galvanometer needle deflects momentarily and then returns to zero as the magnet passes through and falls away.

(ii) State any effect on the magnetic field produced by the coil. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

The induced current in the coil produces its own magnetic field. As the N pole approaches, an N pole is induced at the top of the coil to oppose the motion. As it falls away, an S pole is induced at the bottom of the coil to oppose the motion.

IGCSE Physics - Chapter 9: Magnets & Currents (9-16)

Question 9 (0625/41_Summer_2018_Q10) - Magnets And Currents

(a) Explain why the voltage of the supply to the primary coil of a transformer must be alternating. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

An alternating voltage is required to produce an alternating current, which in turn creates a changing magnetic field. This changing field is necessary to induce a voltage in the secondary coil.

(b) Fig. 10.1 shows a transformer.

There are 8000 turns in the primary coil of the transformer. The primary coil is connected to a 240 V mains supply. A 6.0V lamp connected to the secondary coil operates at full brightness.

(i) Calculate the number of turns in the secondary coil. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Ns ⁄ Np = Vs ⁄ Vp

Ns = Np × (Vs ⁄ Vp) = 8000 × (6.0 ⁄ 240)

Number of turns = 200.

(ii) The current in the lamp is 2.0A. The transformer operates with 100% efficiency. Calculate the current in the primary circuit. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

IpVp = IsVs

Ip = (IsVs) ⁄ Vp = (2.0A × 6.0V) ⁄ 240V

Current = 0.050 A.

(iii) The primary circuit contains a 2A fuse. Calculate the maximum number of lamps, identical to the lamp in (ii), that can be connected in parallel in the secondary circuit without blowing the fuse. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

The maximum primary current is 2A. Each lamp draws 0.050A from the primary.

Number of lamps = Total current ⁄ Current per lamp = 2A ⁄ 0.050A

Number of lamps = 40.

Question 10 (0625/43_Summer_2018_Q10) - Magnets And Currents

(a) A bar magnet is held with its N-pole just inside one end of a coil. Fig. 10.1 shows the coil connected to a galvanometer that has the zero mark in the centre of the scale.

The magnet is pulled horizontally to the right at a constant speed through a large distance.

(i) State what happens to the galvanometer reading as time passes. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

The galvanometer shows a reading as the magnet is pulled out, and then the reading returns to zero once the magnet is far away.

(ii) As the magnet moves, an N-pole is produced at the left-hand end L of the coil. Explain why the pole at L is an N-pole. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

According to Lenz's law, the induced magnetic field opposes the change that causes it. As the S-pole of the magnet moves away from end L, an N-pole is induced to attract the S-pole and oppose its removal.

(b) A transformer has NP turns on the primary coil and NS turns on the secondary coil. The transformer is used in a school laboratory as a 12V alternating current (a.c.) supply. The transformer is powered from the 240 V a.c. mains supply.

(i) Determine the turns ratio NP⁄NS of the transformer. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

NP ⁄ NS = VP ⁄ VS = 240V ⁄ 12V

Turns ratio = 20 or 20:1.

(ii) The laboratory 12 V a.c. supply is rectified to produce a direct current (d.c.) supply. Underline the component that the rectification circuit must include. [1]

AND gate     diode     NOT gate     potentiometer     thermistor

Tap to reveal answer

A rectification circuit must include a diode.

Question 11 (0625/42_Winter_2018_Q9) - Magnets And Currents

Fig. 9.1 shows a permanent bar magnet next to a circuit that contains a coil and a galvanometer.

(a) Suggest a metal from which the magnet is made. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

The magnet is made from a hard magnetic material like steel.

(b) The magnet is moved to the left and inserted a small distance into the coil. The galvanometer deflects briefly and shows that there is a current in the coil.

(i) Explain why there is a current in the coil. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

As the magnet moves, its magnetic field lines cut the coil. This induces an e.m.f. (voltage) which drives a current through the complete circuit.

(ii) As the magnet is moving near to the coil, end Q of the coil behaves as a magnetic pole. State the polarity of end Q and explain why it has this polarity. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

End Q becomes an N-pole. This is because the induced magnetic field repels or opposes the approaching N-pole of the magnet, according to Lenz's law.

(c) Suggest two ways in which the deflection of the galvanometer can be reversed. [2]

Tap to reveal answer
  1. Withdraw the N-pole from end Q (move the magnet to the right).
  2. Insert the S-pole into end Q.
Question 12 (0625/43_Winter_2018_Q9) - Electricity, Magnets And Currents

(a) Describe how a direct current (d.c.) differs from an alternating current (a.c.). [1]

Tap to reveal answer

A direct current (d.c.) has a constant value and flows in only one direction, whereas an alternating current (a.c.) continuously changes direction.

(b) Fig. 9.1 shows how the voltage output of an a.c. generator varies with time.

A heater is connected directly to the a.c. generator and the maximum current in the heater is 0.75A.

(i) On Fig. 9.2, sketch a graph to indicate how the current in the heater varies with time. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

The graph should be a sinusoidal curve that is in phase with the voltage graph, having the same frequency and reaching a maximum value of 0.75A.

(ii) Calculate the power produced by the heater when the current is 0.75A. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

From Fig 9.1, when the current is max (0.75A), the voltage is max (7.2V).

P = V × I = 7.2V × 0.75A

Power = 5.4 W.

(c) Fig. 9.3 shows the coil ABCD of the a.c. generator between two magnetic poles.

(i) On Fig. 9.3, draw a straight arrow to indicate the direction in which side AB of the coil is moving. Label this arrow M. [1]

(ii) Deduce the direction of the current induced in side AB of the coil and explain your reasoning. [2]

(iii) The rate at which the coil of the a.c. generator rotates increases. State two ways in which the alternating voltage changes. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

(i) Arrow M on side AB should be pointing vertically upwards.

(ii) The current is induced from A to B. This is determined using Fleming's Right-Hand Rule, where the thumb (Motion) points up, the first finger (Field) points from N to S, and the second finger (Current) points from A to B.

(iii) 1. The maximum voltage (amplitude) becomes greater. 2. The frequency becomes greater (or the time period becomes smaller).

Question 13 (0625/41_Winter_2018_Q10) - Magnets And Currents

A transformer consists of two coils of wire wound on a metal core. Fig. 10.1 represents the transformer.

(a) State the name of the metal from which the core is made. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

The core is made of soft iron.

(b) The primary coil of the transformer is connected to the output voltage of an a.c. generator which supplies an alternating current.

(i) Explain why there is a voltage between the two terminals of the secondary coil. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

The alternating magnetic field from the primary coil is linked to the secondary coil via the core. This changing magnetic field cuts the secondary coil, inducing an e.m.f. (voltage).

(ii) There are 560 turns on the primary coil and 910 turns on the secondary coil of the transformer. The voltage between the two terminals of the secondary coil is 78 V. Calculate the voltage of the a.c. generator. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Vp ⁄ Vs = Np ⁄ Ns

Vp = Vs × (Np ⁄ Ns) = 78V × (560 ⁄ 910)

Generator voltage = 48 V.

(c) Transformers are used to increase the voltage when electrical energy is transmitted in cables across long distances. Explain why power losses in the cables are lower when the voltage is high. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

For the same power, a higher voltage means a lower current. Since power loss in cables is given by I2R, a lower current means less power loss as heat.

Question 14 (0625/41_Summer_2019_Q8) - Magnets And Currents

A student turns the handle of an alternating current (a.c.) generator and the coil rotates. Fig. 8.1 represents the structure of the a.c. generator.

(a) There is an alternating voltage output between the two terminals.

(i) Explain why rotating the coil produces an output voltage. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

As the coil rotates in the magnetic field, the wires of the coil cut the magnetic field lines. This induces an e.m.f. (voltage) across the ends of the coil by electromagnetic induction.

(ii) State the position of the rotating coil when the alternating output voltage is at a maximum value and explain why the maximum output occurs at this position. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

The output voltage is maximum when the plane of the coil is horizontal. In this position, the sides of the coil are moving vertically and cutting the magnetic field at the fastest rate.

(b) A lamp and an open switch are connected in series to the output terminals of the a.c. generator. The switch is closed and the lamp lights up. The student has to apply a greater force on the handle. Explain why a greater force is needed to keep the lamp lit. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

When the lamp is lit, there is a current in the coil. This current flowing in the magnetic field experiences a force that opposes the rotation (Lenz's Law). Therefore, the student must apply a greater force to do more work and supply the energy for the lamp.

Question 15 (0625/42_Summer_2019_Q9) - Magnets And Currents

(a) Describe how to demagnetise a bar magnet using alternating current (a.c.) in a coil. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

First, place the magnet inside the coil. Then, switch on the a.c. power supply. Finally, with the power still on, gradually withdraw the magnet from the coil to a large distance.

(b) Fig. 9.1 shows a simple direct current (d.c.) motor.

(i) Explain the purpose of the split-ring commutator. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

The purpose is to keep the coil rotating in the same direction by changing the direction of the current in the coil every half cycle (180 degrees).

(ii) The voltage of the power supply is increased. State the effect this has on the motor. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

The coil will rotate faster.

Question 16 (0625/43_Summer_2019_Q10) - Magnets And Currents

Fig. 10.1 shows a simple alternating current generator.

(a) On Fig. 10.2, sketch a graph to show how the electromotive force (e.m.f.) induced varies with time for one revolution of the coil. Assume that the coil starts in the horizontal position, as shown in Fig. 10.1. Label the points on the time axis where the coil has completed 1/4 revolution and 3/4 revolution. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

The graph should show a correct sine/cosine shape starting from a maximum voltage. It should pass through zero at the points labelled 1/4 revolution and 3/4 revolution.

(b) Explain why an e.m.f. is induced only when the coil is turning. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

An e.m.f. is induced only when the coil is cutting magnetic field lines, which only happens when it is turning.

(c) State the name of the components labelled P and Q and state their purpose. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Name: Slip rings.

Purpose: To provide a continuous connection to the external circuit while the coil is rotating.

(d) State two possible changes that cause a larger e.m.f. to be induced. [2]

Tap to reveal answer
  1. Increase the strength of the magnetic field.
  2. Increase the speed of rotation of the coil.

IGCSE Physics - Chapter 9: Magnets & Currents (17-24)

Question 17 (0625/42_Winter_2019_Q7) - Electricity, Magnets And Currents

(a) Fig. 7.1 shows a coil of wire wound on a thin plastic cylinder. The plastic has no effect on any magnetic field. The galvanometer is extremely sensitive.

A magnet is fixed to a small trolley that runs without friction on a track through the cylinder and coil.

(i) The trolley is released from point A so it runs through the coil from right to left. State and explain what is observed on the galvanometer. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

The galvanometer shows a deflection and then a reverse deflection. This is because a voltage is induced as the magnet enters the coil, and then an opposite voltage is induced as it leaves the coil, due to the change of magnetic flux.

(ii) The trolley is now released from point B so it runs through the coil from right to left again. State what is observed on the galvanometer and explain why it is different to your answer in (a)(i). [2]

Tap to reveal answer

A larger deflection is observed because the trolley moves at a higher speed. This causes a larger rate of change of magnetic flux, inducing a larger voltage.

(b) Fig. 7.2 shows an extension lead used to supply power to a 3kW electric heater on a cool evening.

State and explain three dangers with this arrangement. [4]

Tap to reveal answer

Danger 1: The extension lead is designed for a 25W lamp but is used for a 3kW heater. This will draw too much current, causing the lead to overheat and potentially cause a fire.

Danger 2: There is a cut in the outer insulation, which could expose live wires and lead to an electric shock.

Danger 3: The plug and socket are lying on damp grass. Water can conduct electricity, creating a risk of a short circuit or electrocution.

Question 18 (0625/43_Winter_2019_Q10) - Magnets And Currents

(a) A magnet and a coil are attached separately to a door and a door frame as shown in Fig. 10.1.

The purpose of the arrangement is to activate a circuit connected to an LED indicator when the door is opening or closing. This will provide a visual indication that the door is being used. Initially, the door is closed and then it is opened.

(i) Explain why the indicator comes on and then goes off when the door is opened. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

As the door opens, the movement of the magnet relative to the coil induces a current, causing the indicator to light up. The light goes off when the magnet stops moving relative to the coil.

(ii) The door shuts. The indicator comes on more brightly but for a shorter time than it did in (i). Suggest and explain why this happens. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

The door closes more quickly than it was opened, resulting in a larger rate of change of magnetic flux. This induces a higher current, making the indicator brighter. The movement occurs over a shorter length of time.

(b) A circuit breaker is recommended for use with an electric lawnmower. State two reasons for this recommendation. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Reason 1: It provides quick response to a surge in current, protecting against electric shock if the cable is cut.

Reason 2: It is easily re-settable, unlike a fuse which needs to be replaced.

Question 19 (0625/41_Summer_2020_Q7) - Magnets And Currents

An electromagnet consists of a solenoid X that is made of copper wire. The solenoid contains an iron core.

(a) Explain why:

(i) the structure of copper makes it a suitable material for the wire [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Copper contains free electrons that are able to move, making it a good electrical conductor.

(ii) iron is a suitable material for the core of an electromagnet. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Iron is a magnetic material that is easily magnetised and demagnetised, making it a good temporary magnet.

(b) Fig. 7.1 shows the electromagnet inside a second solenoid Y.

(i) Describe and explain what happens in solenoid Y when solenoid X is connected to an alternating current (a.c.) power supply. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

The a.c. in solenoid X produces an alternating magnetic field. This changing field induces an alternating electromotive force (e.m.f.) across the terminals of solenoid Y through electromagnetic induction.

(ii) A switch and a lamp are connected in series with the terminals of solenoid Y. When the switch is closed, the lamp lights up at normal brightness. Describe and explain what happens to the current in solenoid X when the switch is closed. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

The current in solenoid X increases. This is because it must now supply the power that is being used by the lamp in solenoid Y.

Question 20 (0625/42_Summer_2020_Q7) - Magnets And Currents

(a) A student makes a transformer that uses an alternating current (a.c.) supply with an electromotive force (e.m.f.) of 12.0V to induce an output potential difference (p.d.) of 2.0V.

The student is provided with two lengths of insulated wire and the U-shaped piece of iron shown in Fig. 7.1.

(i) Complete and label Fig. 7.1 to show the transformer connected to the supply and the output from the transformer. [3]

(ii) Explain the function of the piece of iron in the transformer. [2]

(iii) The output of the transformer is connected to a lamp. The current in the lamp is 100mA. The transformer is 100% efficient. Calculate the input current to the transformer. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

(i) The diagram should show a primary coil wound around the iron core and connected to the 12V supply. A secondary coil should also be wound around the core, with significantly fewer coils than the primary, connected to the output.

(ii) The iron core links the magnetic fields of the two coils and concentrates the field, ensuring a stronger magnetic field in the secondary for better induction.

(iii)

VpIp = VsIs

Ip = (VsIs) ⁄ Vp = (2.0V × 0.10A) ⁄ 12.0V

Input current = 0.017 A.

(b) Another transformer is used in a school laboratory to step down a mains supply with a p.d. of 110V to 12V. This transformer is mounted in a metal case. State and explain an essential safety feature required for this arrangement. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

The metal case must be earthed. This is a safety precaution in case a live wire touches the case, which would prevent the case from becoming live and causing an electric shock.

Question 21 (0625/43_Summer_2020_Q9) - Magnets And Currents

Fig. 9.1 shows a simple direct current (d.c.) electric motor. The coil rotates about the axis when there is a current in the coil. The coil is connected to the rest of the circuit by the brushes.

(a) (i) On Fig. 9.1, draw a pair of arrows to show which way the coil rotates. Explain the direction you have chosen. [3]

(ii) On Fig. 9.1, draw an arrow to show the direction in which electrons flow through the coil. [1]

(iii) Explain why the electrons flow in the direction you have shown in (a)(ii). [1]

Tap to reveal answer

(i) The coil rotates anti-clockwise. The force is down on the left and up on the right, as determined by Fleming's Left-Hand Rule.

(ii) The arrow should show electron flow from the negative terminal to the positive terminal.

(iii) Electrons are negatively charged and are repelled from the negative connection of the supply.

(b) State any difference each of the following changes makes to the rotation of the coil in Fig. 9.1:

(i) changing the polarity of the power supply to that shown in Fig. 9.2 [1]

(ii) changing the coil to the new coil shown in Fig. 9.3 [1]

(iii) using a stronger magnetic field. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

(i) The coil now rotates in the opposite direction (clockwise).

(ii) The coil turns faster due to a greater turning effect.

(iii) The coil turns faster due to a greater turning effect.

Question 22 (0625/41_Winter_2020_Q7) - Magnets And Currents, Atoms And Radioactivity

(a) A permanent magnet is made from only one material. Underline the material from which it is possible to make a permanent magnet. [1]

aluminium    copper    soft iron    mercury    plastic    steel    uranium

Tap to reveal answer

A permanent magnet is made from steel.

(b) An electron source produces a narrow beam of electrons that all travel at the same speed. The electron source is placed in a vacuum and the beam of electrons travels vertically downwards. Fig. 7.1 shows the beam of electrons before it passes between the N-pole and the S-pole of a magnet.

(i) Describe what is meant by the direction of a magnetic field. State the direction of the magnetic field between the two poles in Fig. 7.1. [1]

(ii) Describe and explain what happens to the beam of electrons in the magnetic field between the poles of the magnet in Fig. 7.1. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

(i) The direction of a magnetic field is the direction of the force on a N-pole. The direction is from left to right (N to S).

(ii) The beam deflects into the page. Moving electrons constitute a current, and a current in a magnetic field experiences a force, as described by Fleming's Left-Hand Rule.

(c) A beam consists of α-particles, β-particles and γ-rays. Explain how a uniform magnetic field may be used to separate the α-particles, the β-particles and the γ-rays. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

When the beam passes through the magnetic field, the α-particles and β-particles deflect in opposite directions because they have opposite charges. The α-particles deflect less due to their greater mass. The γ-rays are uncharged and therefore do not deflect.

Question 23 (0625/42_Winter_2020_Q9) - Magnets And Currents

(a) Fig. 9.1 shows a bar magnet and four plotting compasses A, B, C and D.

On Fig. 9.1:

(i) draw an arrow on each of the three plotting compasses B, C and D to show the direction of the magnetic field [2]

(ii) label the magnetic poles of the bar magnet N and S. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

(i) Compass C should point horizontally to the right. Compasses B and D should point horizontally to the left.

(ii) The left end of the magnet is S and the right end is N.

Tap to reveal answer

Place the magnet in a solenoid carrying an a.c. current and then either withdraw the magnet or decrease the current slowly to zero.

(i) The pattern should be at least three concentric circles, with the lines closer together near the wire. Arrows should show a clockwise direction.

(ii) Reversing the current reverses the direction of the magnetic field.

Question 24 (0625/43_Winter_2020_Q9) - Magnets And Currents

(a) Electrical power is produced in a power station by an alternating current (a.c.) generator. The output of the generator has a voltage of 22000 V. The electrical power is transmitted at a voltage of 400 000 V. Explain why electrical power is transmitted at a voltage of 400 000 V and not 22 000 V. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Transmitting at a high voltage results in a low current for the same power. Since heat loss depends on the current squared (P=I2R), this leads to less power loss in the transmission lines.

(b) A computer contains a transformer. The input voltage to the transformer is 240V. The output voltage from the transformer is 20V and the output current is 2.3A. The efficiency of the transformer is 90%. Calculate the input current to the transformer. [5]

Tap to reveal answer

Power output = Vs × Is = 20V × 2.3A = 46W

Efficiency = (Power output ⁄ Power input) × 100%

Power input = Power output ⁄ Efficiency = 46W ⁄ 0.90 = 51.1W

Input current = Power input ⁄ Vp = 51.1W ⁄ 240V

Input current = 0.21 A.

(ii) Explain why the needle comes to rest in this position. [2]

The compass needle itself is a small magnet, and it aligns with the direction of the magnetic field it is in. The North pole of the needle is attracted to the South pole of the main magnet because unlike poles attract.

Question 26 (0625/42_Summer_2021_Q8) - Atoms And Radioactivity, Magnets And Currents

(a) Two identical radioactive sources emit α-particles and γ-rays into two vacuum tubes.

(i) Fig. 8.1 shows two electrically charged plates on either side of one of the vacuum tubes.

Write the symbol α once in Table 8.1 to indicate any deflection of the α-particles. Write the symbol γ once in Table 8.1 to indicate any deflection of the γ-rays. [2]

Table 8.1
into page out of page no deflection towards bottom of page towards top of page
Tap to reveal answer

α-particles are positively charged, so they will be deflected towards the bottom of the page (towards the -2500 V plate). γ-rays are uncharged, so they will experience no deflection.

(ii) Fig. 8.2 shows the poles of a very strong magnet on either side of the other vacuum tube.

Write the symbol α once in Table 8.2 to indicate any deflection of the α-particles. Write the symbol γ once in Table 8.2 to indicate any deflection of the γ-rays. [2]

Table 8.2
into page out of page no deflection towards bottom of page towards top of page
Tap to reveal answer

γ-rays are uncharged, so they will experience no deflection. α-particles are positive charges moving to the right (a current to the right). Using Fleming's Left-Hand Rule with the field pointing up (N to S), the force is into the page.

(b) Fig. 8.3 shows a simple direct current (d.c.) electric motor with a split-ring commutator.

(i) State and explain the direction of rotation of the coil as seen from point X. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

Statement: The coil will rotate clockwise.

Explanation: Using Fleming's Left-Hand Rule, the force on the left-hand wire of the coil is upwards, and the force on the right-hand wire is downwards. This pair of forces creates a clockwise turning moment.

(ii) The coil rotates through 90° from the position shown. State what happens to the moment in this position. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

When the coil is vertical, the moment becomes zero.

(iii) The coil is rotated through 180° from the position shown. By considering the forces on the coil, explain how the split-ring commutator enables the motor to turn continuously. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

After 180° rotation, the split-ring commutator reverses the direction of the current in the coil. This ensures that the wire that is now on the left still experiences an upward force and the wire on the right experiences a downward force, allowing the coil to continue rotating in the same direction.

Question 27 (0625/43_Summer_2021_Q9) - Magnets And Currents

(a) An X-ray machine requires a supply of 110kV. The mains electricity supply is 230V. A transformer is used to supply the correct voltage to the X-ray machine. There are 50 turns on the primary coil of the transformer. Calculate the number of turns on the secondary coil. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Ns ⁄ Np = Vs ⁄ Vp

Ns = Np × (Vs ⁄ Vp) = 50 × (110000 V ⁄ 230 V) ≈ 23913

Number of turns = 24000 (rounded).

(b) Draw a labelled diagram of a step-down transformer. On the labels, state a suitable material for each of the components. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

The diagram should show:

  • A soft iron core (typically a rectangular loop).
  • A primary coil made of copper wire with a larger number of turns.
  • A secondary coil made of copper wire with a fewer number of turns than the primary.

(c) Explain how a transformer operates. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

An alternating voltage in the primary coil drives an alternating current, which produces a changing magnetic field in the soft iron core. The core guides this changing field to the secondary coil. The changing magnetic flux cutting through the secondary coil induces an alternating voltage across it.

Question 28 (0625/43_Winter_2021_Q10) - Magnets And Currents

(a) A transformer has 500 turns on the primary coil and 25 turns on the secondary coil. The input voltage is 120V.

(i) Calculate the output voltage. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Vs = Vp × (Ns ⁄ Np) = 120 V × (25 ⁄ 500)

Output voltage = 6.0 V.

(ii) The current in the primary coil is 125 mA. The transformer is 100% efficient. Calculate the output current. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

IsVs = IpVp

Is = (IpVp) ⁄ Vs = (0.125 A × 120 V) ⁄ 6.0 V

Output current = 2.5 A.

(b) Fig. 10.1 shows a loose wire connected in a circuit with a d.c. (direct current) power supply and a switch. The length of the wire between the two supports is in the magnetic field of a horseshoe magnet. The power supply is switched on and the wire moves down.

(i) On Fig. 10.1, draw an arrow on the wire to show the direction of the current. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

Using Fleming's Left-Hand Rule, with the Force downwards and the Field from N to S, the current must flow from right to left across the loose part of the wire.

(ii) The power supply is switched off and the wire returns to its original position. The power supply is then switched on so that the current is in the opposite direction. State and explain what happens to the wire. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

The wire moves up. Reversing the direction of the current reverses the direction of the force on the wire.

(c) A split-ring commutator is an important feature of a d.c. motor. Suggest one reason why the d.c. motor cannot operate without a split-ring commutator. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

Without it, the motor would not continue to rotate in the same direction after completing a half turn, as the direction of the turning force would reverse.

Question 29 (0625/42_Summer_2022_Q7) - Magnets And Currents

Fig. 7.1 shows a small plotting compass which is aligned with the magnetic field between magnetic poles A and B of a U-shaped magnet.

(a) State the polarity of the poles. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

The N of the compass points towards the S pole. Therefore, pole A is N and pole B is S.

(b) Fig. 7.2 shows a wire, placed between two poles, carrying a current in the direction of the arrow. On Fig. 7.2, draw an arrow to show the direction of the force on the wire due to the magnetic field. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Using Fleming's Left-Hand Rule, with the magnetic field from N to S (left to right) and the current flowing into the page, the force on the wire is vertically upwards.

(c) Fig. 7.3 shows a β-particle moving in the direction of the arrow between the same two poles. On Fig. 7.3, draw an arrow to show the direction of the force on the β-particle due to the magnetic field. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

A β-particle is negatively charged, so its motion to the right is equivalent to a conventional current to the left. Using Fleming's Left-Hand Rule, with the field from N to S and the current to the left, the force is vertically downwards.

Question 30 (0625/43_Summer_2022_Q9) - Magnets And Currents

(a) Fig. 9.1 shows a magnet on the end of a spring and a coil of wire connected to a sensitive centre-zero galvanometer. The magnet can move freely through the coil.

(i) The magnet is pulled down and released. Describe and explain what happens to the needle of the sensitive galvanometer. [4]

Tap to reveal answer

The needle of the galvanometer oscillates back and forth. As the magnet moves up and down, the coil cuts the magnetic field lines. This induces a changing voltage and hence a changing current in the coil. The induced current flows in one direction as the magnet moves down and in the opposite direction as it moves up.

(ii) The magnet is replaced with a stronger magnet. State the effect of using a stronger magnet on what happens to the needle of the galvanometer. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

Using a stronger magnet will produce a larger (maximum) deflection of the needle.

(b) A step-up transformer is used to step up the output voltage of a power station from 25000 V to 400000V for transmission along power lines. The number of turns on the secondary coil is 36000. Calculate the number of turns on the primary coil. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Np ⁄ Ns = Vp ⁄ Vs

Np = Ns × (Vp ⁄ Vs) = 36000 × (25000 V ⁄ 400000 V)

Number of turns = 2250.

Question 32 (0625/43_Winter_2022_Q11) - Magnets And Currents

(a) Fig. 11.1 shows a solenoid connected to a battery. On Fig. 11.1, draw the pattern of the magnetic field inside and around the solenoid. Indicate the direction of the magnetic field with an arrow. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

The magnetic field pattern should resemble that of a bar magnet. Inside the solenoid, the field lines should be straight, parallel lines. Outside, they should loop around from one end to the other. Using the right-hand grip rule, the top of the solenoid is a N pole, so the arrows should point upwards inside the solenoid and emerge from the top, looping around to enter the bottom.

(b) Electrical power is transmitted at a voltage of 400kV. A transformer reduces the voltage to 33kV for use by heavy industry in large factories. The number of turns on the primary coil of the transformer is 11000. Calculate the number of turns on the secondary coil of the transformer. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Ns ⁄ Np = Vs ⁄ Vp

Ns = Np × (Vs ⁄ Vp) = 11000 × (33000 V ⁄ 400000 V) = 907.5

Number of turns = 910 (rounded to a whole number).

Question 33 (0625/41_Summer_2023_Q8) - Magnets And Currents

The electricity supplied to a town is transmitted using a high-voltage cable. A transformer in the town has a soft-iron core.

(a) Explain the principle of operation of a simple iron-cored transformer. [4]

Tap to reveal answer

An alternating current in the primary coil generates a changing magnetic field in the iron core. The soft iron core concentrates and transfers this magnetic field to the secondary coil. As the secondary coil cuts this changing magnetic field, an e.m.f. is induced across it.

(b) The transformer steps the supply voltage down from 220000 V to 33000 V.

(i) There are 450 turns on the secondary coil. Calculate the number of turns on the primary coil. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Np ⁄ Ns = Vp ⁄ Vs

Np = Ns × (Vp ⁄ Vs) = 450 × (220000 ⁄ 33000)

Number of turns = 3000.

(ii) The electrical power transferred to the transformer by the high-voltage cable is 77MW. Calculate the current in the primary coil. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

P = I × V

I = P ⁄ V = 77,000,000 W ⁄ 220,000 V

Current = 350 A.

Question 34 (0625/42_Summer_2023_Q8) - Electricity, Magnets And Currents

(a) (i) State what is meant by a magnetic field. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

A magnetic field is a region in which a magnetic pole experiences a force.

(ii) Define the direction of a magnetic field. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

The direction of a magnetic field is defined as the direction of the force on a North pole.

(b) Fig. 8.1 shows a negatively charged metal sphere. On Fig. 8.1, draw four lines to show the electric field and its direction. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

The drawing should show four radial lines pointing towards the sphere, equally spaced around it.

(c) Fig. 8.2 shows a circuit.

The three cells are identical and have zero resistance. The resistors R₁, R₂, and R₃ are identical. The reading on the voltmeter is 6.0V. When the diode is conducting, it has zero resistance and zero potential difference (p.d.) across it.

(i) Determine the e.m.f. of one cell. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

The voltmeter reads the total e.m.f. of the three cells. The e.m.f. of one cell is 6.0 V ⁄ 3 = 2.0 V.

(ii) Determine the ratio of the p.d. across R₂ to the p.d. across R₃. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

The ratio of the potential difference is 1:2.

(iii) All the cells are reversed.

1. State the change in current in R₁. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

The diode is now in the wrong direction and will not allow current to pass. Therefore, the current in R₁ becomes zero.

2. Determine the new value of the ratio of the p.d. across R₂ to the p.d. across R₃. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

With no current in the R₁ branch, R₂ and R₃ are in series. Since they are identical, they will have the same potential difference across them. The new ratio is 1:1.

Question 35 (0625/43_Summer_2023_Q7) - Magnets And Currents

The voltage across the primary coil of a 100% efficient transformer is 220 V and the voltage across the secondary coil is 12V.

(a) The current in the secondary coil is 2.5A. Calculate the current in the primary coil. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

Vp × Ip = Vs × Is

Ip = (Vs × Is) ⁄ Vp = (12 V × 2.5 A) ⁄ 220 V

Current = 0.14 A.

Tap to reveal answer

Np ⁄ Ns = Vp ⁄ Vs = 220 V ⁄ 12 V

Question 36 (0625/43_Winter_2023_Q8) - Magnets And Currents

(a) Fig. 8.1 shows the single turn coil of a simple direct current (d.c.) motor.

(i) Explain the direction of the turning effect as seen by an observer at O. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

The turning effect is clockwise. Using Fleming's Left-Hand Rule, the force on the left side of the coil is upwards, while the force on the right side is downwards, creating a clockwise moment.

(ii) The coil is replaced by an otherwise identical new coil with three turns and the same current in the coil. State how the turning effect compares with the turning effect in (i). [1]

Tap to reveal answer

With more turns, the turning effect is greater.

(iii) A third coil is identical to the coil in (i) except that its resistance is three times greater. The potential difference (p.d.) across the coil is the same as the p.d. in (i). State how the turning effect compares with the turning effect in (i). [1]

Tap to reveal answer

With three times the resistance, the current (I=V⁄R) will be one-third of the original. Since the force is proportional to the current, the turning effect is less.

Tap to reveal answer

(iii) Draw an end view of the position of the plane of the coil at time t₃. Include the labels A and B. [1]
